opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it really comes down to two things: how big the impact of AI could be, and how quickly it seems to be arriving.

If you look at the trajectory of these models over the last several years, every time we scale up compute and data, we get systems that can do things the previous generation couldn't. It's quite plausible that at some point we'll have systems that can do most of the work humans do, including scientific research and AI research itself. That could be enormously good. You could imagine dramatically accelerating progress on disease, energy, poverty. But a technology that powerful is also one where getting it wrong could be really bad.

The core worry is that we don't yet have reliable ways to make sure these systems do what we intend. Right now we train models, look at their behavior, and if it seems fine we deploy them. That works okay when the models are weaker than us and we can check their work. It gets much harder once they're doing things we can't easily evaluate, or once they're capable enough that subtle misalignment in their goals actually matters. There's also the misuse side: very capable systems could help people do things like build biological weapons or carry out large-scale cyberattacks, and we need safeguards in place before those capabilities show up, not after.

What makes it feel urgent to me is that I don't think the timelines are necessarily long. If transformative AI is decades away, we have time to figure this out gradually. But if it's a handful of years away, then the research on alignment, interpretability, evaluations, and responsible scaling policies has to happen now. And it's a field where relatively few people have been working on these problems compared to how many are working on making the systems more capable. So the marginal person working on safety can make a real difference.

So: potentially the most consequential technology we've ever built, real uncertainty about whether we can control it, possibly not much time, and not many people working on it. That combination is why I think it's one of the most important things to work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI’s potentially enormous impact but does not imagine each person directing a million-person company of exceptionally smart members.

r002.rationale: It says relatively few people work on safety problems compared with those advancing AI capabilities, and that this makes each safety researcher’s contribution significant.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way I'd put it is: I expect AI to be one of the most transformative technologies humanity has ever built, and possibly the most transformative. And when you believe that, the question of whether it goes well or badly becomes incredibly high stakes.

I came to this in a somewhat gradual way. When I started working in machine learning, I was mostly excited about the capabilities side, about what these systems could do. But as I watched models get more capable year over year, I kept updating toward thinking the timelines were shorter than I'd assumed, and that we really didn't have a good understanding of how these systems work internally or how to reliably get them to do what we want.

And that combination worries me. You have systems that are becoming more general, more autonomous, more economically useful, and so there's enormous pressure to deploy them widely. At the same time, our tools for understanding them and steering them are pretty immature. We can't look inside a model and confidently say what it's going to do in a situation it hasn't seen before. We train these things with fairly blunt methods, and we're often surprised by the behaviors that come out.

So the case for safety work isn't really about any one specific scenario. It's more that if you're building something that might eventually be smarter than us in many domains, you want to have done the work ahead of time to make sure it's trustworthy, that it's honest, that it doesn't pursue goals we didn't intend. And you don't want to be figuring that out after the fact, because some of these mistakes could be very hard to recover from.

The other thing I'd say is that I think this is actually tractable. It's not just worrying from the sidelines. There's real technical work to do: interpretability, alignment research, evaluations that tell you what a model is capable of before you deploy it, building the institutional practices so that labs make careful decisions as capabilities scale. A lot of that is still early, which means individual people can have a disproportionate impact right now. That's a pretty rare combination, high stakes and genuine room to contribute, and it's why I think it's one of the most important things someone could work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as potentially humanity’s most transformative technology, but does not illustrate this with everyone directing a million-person company staffed by the smartest people they know.

r002.rationale: It says the work is early and individuals can have disproportionate impact, but does not state that the number of people working on AI safety is small relative to the problem’s scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic reason is that AI could become extraordinarily powerful, and we don’t yet know how to make sure that power is reliably used in ways that benefit people. If we build systems that can do most of the intellectual work humans do, that could lead to enormous advances in science and medicine. But it also means the consequences of mistakes or misuse could be much larger than they are with today’s software.

One concern is that a system could be very capable without actually pursuing the goals we intended. Being good at solving problems isn’t the same thing as understanding when it should stop, ask for permission, or accept correction. And if we’re delegating increasingly consequential decisions to these systems, we need more than the observation that they usually behave well in testing.

So, for me, AI safety is about closing that gap: making sure our ability to understand and control these systems keeps up with our ability to build them. You don’t have to be certain that things will go badly to think that’s worth working on. Even a relatively small chance of a very large catastrophe deserves serious attention, especially when work now could help prevent it.

r001.rationale: The response describes powerful AI and major potential advances, but does not imagine each person directing a million-person company of exceptionally smart members.

r002.rationale: It argues that AI safety deserves serious attention, but does not say that few people work on AI safety relative to the problem's scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could become one of the most consequential technologies we ever build. If we develop systems that can do most of the intellectual work humans do, that could bring enormous benefits, but it could also create risks that we’re poorly prepared to manage.

The concern is that making a system more capable doesn’t automatically make it reliable, controllable, or aligned with what people actually want. And as we give these systems more responsibility, mistakes could become much harder to reverse.

So AI safety seems important because there’s a lot at stake, and we still have fundamental questions to answer about how to make these systems behave safely. Working on those questions now could substantially improve our chances of getting the benefits of AI while avoiding the worst outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response mentions systems that could do most human intellectual work, but does not describe each person directing a million-person company or its members being as smart as the smartest people they know.

r002.rationale: The response says fundamental safety questions remain, but does not state that the number of people working on AI safety is small relative to the problem.
